1373.title: Blessing the house
1373.hook: many churches bless homes at Epiphany or when people move in
1373.howItsDone: Some Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran households chalk their doors at Epiphany; Orthodox priests visit homes with water blessed at Theophany; and other churches offer a house blessing when a family moves in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the icon corner, a small place set apart for prayer. Your line was a corner of heaven.

Above a door, in white chalk, a short line of numbers and letters with little crosses between them. It went up one winter afternoon, while someone stood on a kitchen chair. A few streets away, a couple has just carried the last box into a new apartment, and their pastor stands in the empty living room, reading a short passage aloud. Across town, an Orthodox priest moves from room to room with a sprig of green dipped in water, sprinkling the walls, the beds, the stove. Three homes. One old habit.

When Jesus sends his followers out to the towns in Luke, he tells them what to do at the door: "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house." First, before teaching or supper. If a person of peace lives there, the peace will rest on them; if not, it comes back to you. Nothing is wasted. Next, the chalk. Around Epiphany, the feast of the wise men, some Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran households mark the door with the year and three letters. Tradition says they stand for the names later given to the wise men, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, and also for Latin words asking Christ to bless the house. Matthew says the wise men came to a house: "when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother." The chalk remembers a house where Christ was found. Then, the water. Orthodox churches bless water at Theophany, the feast of Christ's baptism, and afterward priests visit homes to sprinkle it through each room, with prayers for the people who live there. Other churches bless a home when a family moves in, room by room. Last, a house that changed. Zacchaeus, a tax collector the crowd grumbles about, climbs a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus invites himself over. By the end, Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house." Not to the bricks: to the man, and the household. Walls don't need peace. The people who argue in that kitchen and make up in it do. A blessing asks that this ordinary place be one where God is welcome.
screen: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly through your home, or walk it in your mind, pausing at the front door and then in each room, thinking of what happens there, and who. If you pray, you can say at each doorway, peace be to this house; if you don't, let each pause be a wish of peace for whoever lives there. End where you started, at the door.
Blessing the house. Asking God's peace on a home and the people in it, with words, chalk or water.
Your line: peace to this house. Peace for the people inside. Until tomorrow.

1374.title: Walking the Camino
1374.hook: hundreds of thousands walk to Santiago every year
1374.howItsDone: Pilgrims walk the Camino de Santiago on several routes across Spain and beyond, carrying a pilgrim's booklet stamped along the way, and some attend the pilgrims' Mass at the cathedral in Santiago when they arrive.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessing the house: chalk, water, and the words Jesus sent to the door. Your line was peace to this house.

Buen camino. Two words, called across a dusty road in northern Spain. A farmer leaning on a gate says it to a passing walker with a backpack. Two strangers share a bench by a fountain, and as one heaves the pack back on, the other says it. A woman behind a café counter hands over a coffee, presses an ink stamp into a little booklet, and says it too. In Spanish it means something like good way, or good road. And this road leads to a cathedral in a city called Santiago de Compostela.

The Camino de Santiago means the Way of Saint James. Back in year three, pilgrims' roads passed through Santiago. Tradition says the apostle James is buried there, and walkers come along several routes. Some start at their own front doors. Some walk for prayer, some for grief, some to think, some without being sure why. Next, that word, way. In John's Gospel, Jesus says, "I am the way, the truth, and the life." In Acts, before the name Christian shows up, Saul goes looking for followers of Jesus, "that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem." The early followers were people of the Way, and for some walkers, wishing a stranger a good way carries that echo. Then Emmaus. On the day of the resurrection, two heartbroken disciples walk out of Jerusalem. "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them." They don't know him. He walks, listens, and opens the scriptures to them. At the village, evening coming on, they beg him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." At supper he breaks the bread, they know him, and he's gone. "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?" Last, the greeting. Some walkers say you don't choose your companions: the stranger who shares water or a bandage may be the one you remember. Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox Christians and people unsure what they believe walk the same road, and buen camino doesn't ask which.

Stand and walk slowly around the room, one step for each breath, heel, then ball, then toes; if you can't stand, press each foot into the floor in turn. If you pray, you can pray with your steps, a word from a psalm or the name of someone you're carrying; if you don't, count the steps and notice the feet that carry you.
Walking the Camino. The pilgrim road to Santiago, the Way of Saint James, where walkers wish each other buen camino.
Your line: buen camino. A good way, wished to whoever walks beside you. Rest well.

fork.reveal: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening." at supper he breaks the bread, and they know him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long hike across Spain.
what it means: a pilgrim road to Santiago, where tradition places the tomb of James, walked as prayer, with strangers.
what a scholar hears: hodos, the way: the early followers were people of "this way," and at Emmaus Jesus was known afterward, "by the way."
recall: the talk that opens up the readings
guess: the pilgrim road to Santiago, the Way of Saint James

a procession around a cathedral on a saint's day

chat.meaning: Buen camino means something like good way. The early followers of Jesus were people of the Way, and for some walkers the greeting carries that echo.

1375.title: Retreats
1375.hook: a few days away for silence and prayer
1375.tomorrow: Block close: the house of prayer
1375.howItsDone: Christians go on retreat at monastery guest houses, retreat centers and church weekends; some follow the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius with a guide, and others keep a single quiet day of silence, prayer and walking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Camino, the long road to Santiago. Your line was buen camino.

A weekend bag by the door, packed light. No laptop in it. Jesus once said to his tired friends, in Mark's Gospel: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." The next line: "for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat." Some Christians take that invitation literally. A weekend in the guest house of a monastery. A few days at a retreat center by a lake. One day in a borrowed room, the phone left in a drawer, nothing on the schedule.
screen: `NO LEISURE SO MUCH AS TO EAT.`
`A GUEST HOUSE, A LAKE, A DRAWER.`

segments.voice: First, Jesus did it himself. Mark says: "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." Luke adds: "And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed." And before he chooses the twelve, Luke says, he goes up a mountain and "continued all night in prayer to God." Second, the surprise. Right after rest a while, they slip off by boat. But the crowd sees them go, runs ahead on foot, and is waiting on the shore. Jesus steps out, and Mark says he "was moved with compassion toward them," and began to teach. The rest was real, and so was the interruption. Third, how Christians go apart now. Some monasteries keep guest rooms, and visitors join the monks at prayer, eat in silence, and walk. Some retreats follow the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, with a guide who meets you each day. Some churches run weekend retreats with talks, singing and long walks; some people keep a single quiet day at home. The shape is the same: leave the noise on purpose, for a while, and then come back. Last, the prophet Elijah, worn out and hiding in a cave, waits for God on a mountain. A great wind tears at the rocks, "but the LORD was not in the wind." Then an earthquake, then a fire, and God isn't in those either. "And after the fire a still small voice." A voice that small is easy to miss in a wind. That's one reason people go on retreat at all.

Plan a quiet day now, a whole day, half a day or a single hour, and pick its date and place: a church, a park, your own kitchen with the phone put away. Decide what you'll leave behind and what you'll bring, a Bible, a notebook, nothing at all. If you pray, offer that day to God now; if you don't, hold the date in mind and let it wait for you.
Retreats. Going apart on purpose, for a day or a few days, for silence and prayer, and then coming back.
Your line: come away awhile. Even Jesus went apart, and then came back. See you soon.

1376.title: Block close: the house of prayer
1376.hook: rites and rooms, bells and bread: faith lives in places and bodies
1376.howItsDone: Christians pray in churches, chapels and meeting houses shaped by their traditions, and at home in prayer corners, at tables and at bedsides; the rites of each church use water, bread, oil, hands, music and silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, retreats: going apart for a while, then coming back. Your line was come away awhile.

Lay out what this stretch of days has put in your hands. Water poured at a font. Oil on a forehead. Bread broken and a cup passed. A bell in a tower. Incense rising. A candle left burning. A hymnal with a cracked spine. Chalk above a door. A shelf in the corner of a room. A boot on a road in Spain. Every one is something you can touch, smell, hear or walk. Faith doesn't live only in the head. It takes up room.

First, the rites. Baptism. Chrismation and confirmation. First communion. The Divine Liturgy and the Mass, a Protestant service, a Quaker meeting held in silence, a Pentecostal service full of sound. The sermon, the creed said together, the peace, the offering, the blessing. Weddings, ordination, anointing the sick, confession, vows. Churches disagree about how many sacraments there are and what happens in them. But each rite does something with a body: water, oil, hands, a bowed head, a handshake of peace. Second, the rooms. The basilica's long hall. The iconostasis, a wall of faces. The gothic cathedral pulling light upward. The plain meeting house with nothing on the walls. Domes like a sky. The table, the pulpit and the font, each set where it is for a reason. A room is a sentence about God, in stone and wood. Third, the arts and the things: bells and the colors of the year, incense and candles, the cross and the crucifix, icons, hymnals, organs, guitars and drums, choirs, churches and crosses from around the world. Then the home: name days, grace at meals, bedtime prayers, the icon corner, the blessing on the door. Then the road: the Camino and the retreat. Last, the title. Isaiah: "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people." Jesus quotes it in the temple, in Mark. And Paul carries the idea into the body: "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?" A building can be a house of prayer; so can a kitchen; and Paul calls the body a temple.
screen: `ROOMS: A SENTENCE IN STONE AND WOOD.`
`A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where prayer, or quiet, or love has been real for you, a church, a grandmother's kitchen, a hospital chapel, a bench by the water, and see the light, the sounds, who was there, and what your body did: kneel, sit, sing, cry, stand still. If you pray, you can thank God for that place; if you don't, let yourself be glad it exists.
Block close. The end of a block on rites, rooms and arts: the ways faith lives in places, things and bodies.
Your line: faith has a body. Rites, rooms, arts and roads: it all takes up room. Block done.

1377.title: Why is there suffering?
1377.hook: Christians have wrestled with this for millennia and offered no easy answer
1377.howItsDone: Christians bring the question of suffering to prayer, to Scripture, especially Job, the Psalms and the cross, and to pastors and friends; churches hold different explanations side by side, and some sit with the question rather than settle it.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the block: the house of prayer. Your line was faith has a body.

"O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" That isn't a skeptic in a debate hall. It's a prophet, Habakkuk, in the opening lines of his book, watching violence and injustice go on while heaven seems quiet. The same question turns up at hospital bedsides, in the late news, at a funeral for someone who died far too young. If God is good, and God is strong, why this? A new block begins, on suffering, doubt and the hardest questions.

Today's word is theodicy: the name philosophers and theologians give to any attempt to show that God is good in a world full of pain. God is good. God is powerful. Terrible things happen, and something seems to have to give. In Luke, people bring Jesus news of Galileans killed by Pilate, and Jesus raises a second disaster himself: a tower in Siloam fell and killed eighteen people. "Think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?" No, he says. In John, his disciples pass a man born blind: "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" Jesus: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents." Twice he refuses the neat equation: you suffer, so you must have done something. Christians have offered answers anyway. Some say God gave people real freedom, and freedom can wound. Some say suffering can refine a person, the way fire tests gold, a picture Peter's first letter uses for faith. Some point to Revelation: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain." And some say the honest thing: we don't know. Some who have sat with deep suffering warn that an answer wise in a classroom can sound cheap at a bedside. No easy answers, but not no answers: Christians do say God is good, and with those who suffer. The days ahead hold that beside the question. If you ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `FREEDOM, FIRE, THE END OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one piece of suffering you can't make sense of, your own, someone else's, or far away, and hold it the way you'd hold someone's hand, without solving it or arguing it away. When a quick answer pops up, set it down. If you pray, you can bring it to God the way Habakkuk did, how long; if you don't, let the question be asked into the quiet, and leave it open.
Theodicy. Any attempt to show that God is good when the world is full of suffering.
Your line: no easy answers. The question is allowed to stay open here. See you tomorrow.

1378.title: Job again
1378.hook: God never explains, but shows up, and Job's friends are rebuked
1378.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Job when they or someone close to them is suffering, and some pastors and chaplains point to the friends' silent week, and their later rebuke, as a pattern for visiting the grieving: be present, and resist explaining.

segments.voice: Yesterday, theodicy: the question of suffering, if God is good. Your line was no easy answers.

The casseroles arrive first. Then the cards. Then the explanations. Everything happens for a reason. At least it was quick. It must have been their time. People mean well. They want to fill a silence that feels unbearable. Back in year two, this path spent a run of days in the book of Job. Today it comes back with one question: what does Job teach about being there for someone who's suffering?

Start with what the friends got right. They came: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." Some readers say the friends never comforted Job better than in that silent week. Then they started talking. Their speeches circle one idea: God is just, so if you're suffering, you must have done something. Job's reply is sharp: "miserable comforters are ye all." He had already told them what would help: "O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom." Then God speaks, out of the whirlwind. You'd expect the explanation at last, the scene in heaven from the first chapter. God never mentions it. Instead God asks questions: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" Not an answer: an encounter. Job, who demanded a hearing, gets one, and goes quiet. Last, the rebuke. God tells Eliphaz, one of the friends: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The friends with their tidy explanations are corrected; Job, who wept and argued and accused, is said to have spoken rightly. Some readers notice the shape: God didn't explain, but showed up; the friends explained, and were rebuked. Explaining feels like helping. Read this way, the book suggests that sitting beside someone, saying nothing, may be the more faithful thing. And if you're the one grieving and ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

Bring to mind someone going through something hard, notice the urge to fix it or find the perfect sentence, and set it down. Then picture one simple way to be there: a visit, a meal left at the door, a message that says only I'm thinking of you, an hour beside them in the quiet. If you pray, you can hold them before God without asking for an explanation; if you don't, hold them in mind, the way the friends sat on the ground.
Job again. The book of Job read for one lesson: God shows up without explaining, and the explaining friends are rebuked.
Your line: show up, don't explain. It's harder than it sounds. I'll be here tomorrow.

1379.title: The darkest psalm (Psalm 88)
1379.hook: a psalm that ends in darkness, and it's still in the Bible
1379.howItsDone: Some Christians pray Psalm 88 in times of grief or depression, and churches that pray the psalms in order, in daily offices, say it along with the others; some pastors point people to it as permission to pray honestly in the dark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job again: God shows up without explaining, and the explaining friends are rebuked. Your line was show up, don't explain.

Open a Bible to Psalm 88, and read the last line first. "Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness." That's the end. No turn. No but I will trust in thee. No hallelujah tacked on at the bottom. The psalm stops in the dark, like a phone call cut off mid-sentence. And it isn't tucked away in a footnote. It sits in the songbook among the psalms of praise, read and sung and copied with the rest.

Start at the top: "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee." Whoever prays this is in the dark, but still talking to someone. That thread holds the whole psalm together. In the middle, the singer feels close to the grave, counted among the dead, forgotten, and throws questions straight at God: "Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?" And: "LORD, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?" No answer comes inside the psalm. Then the ending. Other lament psalms turn near the end, as Psalm 13 did back on day one hundred five: but I have trusted, I will sing. This one doesn't. The heading names Heman the Ezrahite, and darkness is the last word, lover and friend gone. So why is it in the Bible? Jewish and Christian communities kept it and prayed it with the rest of the psalms. Some readers say that's the point: the Bible makes room for a prayer with no happy ending. Someone in long grief, in depression, awake in the small hours, can find their own words already here, already counted as prayer. Other readers notice that you don't keep crying day and night to someone you think isn't there. For them, the cry is itself a kind of trust. Not fixed first, not tidied: prayed, as it is. If the dark is heavy on you, tell someone you trust; and if you ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

Let something still dark come to mind, a loss not healed, a question not answered, a fear that hasn't left, and say it silently as it is, with no silver lining, letting it end where it ends. If you pray, you can say it to God the way Psalm 88 does, even if the last word is darkness; if you don't, say it to the quiet, and rest in the plain fact that it's been said.
The darkest psalm. Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in darkness, and was kept and prayed all the same.
Your line: even darkness can be prayed. Nothing has to be tidied up first. Go gently.

chat.says: Is it okay to pray when I've got nothing hopeful to say at all?
options: Yes. Psalm 88 ends in darkness, with no happy turn, and it was kept as prayer.
Better to wait until you feel hopeful; prayers in the Bible always end on praise.
Only if you add a hopeful line at the end, the way every psalm is written.
chat.meaning: Psalm 88 begins with God of my salvation and ends in darkness, and communities kept praying it. Even darkness can be prayed.
